items.prompt: Big-O names what about a function of n?
choices: The dominant growth term as n grows large
The exact millisecond runtime on your laptop
items.whyRight: Asymptotic upper bound on growth, ignoring lower-order terms and constants.
whyWrong: Wall-clock times include machine noise and constants.
Best case is a different bound (Ω often).
Constants matter in practice but are not what big-O highlights.

items.prompt: Amortized O(1) append on a dynamic array means?
choices: Average cost per append across a sequence, including rare resizes
Every single append is strictly O(1) worst case
items.whyRight: Expensive copies are charged across many cheap appends.
whyWrong: A single resize is O(n); amortization spreads it.
n appends cost linear total, not constant.

items.prompt: O(n log n) vs O(n²) for n = 10⁶ — which statement is safest?
choices: n log n stays practical far longer than n²
items.whyRight: Quadratic blows up; n log n is the usual sort/scan sweet spot.
whyWrong: They differ by a huge factor.
Quadratic is slower for large n.

choices: Extra memory beyond the input representation (unless asked otherwise)
items.whyRight: Clarify with the interviewer; default is auxiliary space.

items.prompt: Saying “this is O(n²) therefore unusable” without n is weak because?
choices: Constants and real n decide practicality
items.whyRight: For tiny n, quadratic can be fine; name n.
whyWrong: Big-O hides constants; it does not forbid discussing them.
It grows with n², not infinity at finite n.

items.whyRight: Master theorem / recursion tree: log n levels each O(n).
whyWrong: Linear would need less work per level or fewer levels.
Exponential is branching without the /2 shrink balanced by linear merge.
